data.summary: Fixed all five reviewer findings (FIG. 1 handle connection, missing depiction of the claimed fluid communication in FIG. 2, FIG. 3 self-contradiction, meta-commentary in the Detailed Description, dangling element in system claim 10) and additionally supplied the missing citation of US-11247858-B2, which was listed in prior_art/INDEX.md but addressed nowhere in the Background. Claims 1-18 substance, the numeral table, and the five-figure plan are otherwise unchanged.
reasoning: The two major findings were real and both were figure-side, not text-side, so I repaired them without touching the claims. FIG. 1 forbade any structure rising from the slab while placing the grip above it, which depicted a detached handle; the disclosure says the device 'may include one or more handles', so joining the grip to the top face adds no matter and removing the contradiction was the correct direction of repair. FIG. 1's opening geometry sentence also had to change from 'a grip well above them' to a grip rising from the top face, or the brief would have contradicted its own numeral entry.

Fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism and the chamber is a limitation of every independent claim, and FIG. 2 affirmatively excluded it ('no particular internal passage or connection route is depicted'). The disclosure states the relationship directly ('in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base') but discloses no through-base opening, duct or exhaust hardware, which earlier repairs correctly stripped out. A single broken line indicating the communication, with an express statement that no passage, duct or opening is depicted, shows the claimed relationship without reinstating unsupported structure. draft/07-drawings.md now lists that relationship among the schematically shown items so the Brief Description and the sheet agree.

Adding the broken line pushed FIG. 2 to 2984 characters, over the 2800 limit, so I condensed redundant geometry wording (leg description, housing placement, 'clear stretch' phrasing) rather than dropping any disclosure-grounded relationship. Final size is 2799. I also amended the chamber 22 endpoint from 'touching no drawn line' to 'clear of the broken line and of the lines bounding the space', because the old target became impossible to satisfy literally once a line crossed the chamber.

The FIG. 3 and Detailed Description findings were pure wording defects and were fixed as suggested. Deleting the motor sentence removes commentary about the document rather than about the invention; no replacement statement is possible because the disclosure says nothing about how vibration is generated, and inventing a motor type or frequency would be unsupported.

Claim 10's transmission path was recited as if it were a component of the system, which is a form inconsistency against claim 1 rather than a scope problem. Recasting it as a 'wherein' clause preserves the identical limitation (rigid path, no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount) while removing the dangling element, so the system claim retains the same distinguishing feature it had before.

The reviewer's ledger stated that 'all four [REF:] identifiers resolve to files', but prior_art/INDEX.md lists five references and US-11247858-B2 was cited nowhere. Every listed reference must be addressed, so I read the reference file and added a Background passage confined to what that file actually says: a horizontal suction plate with a perforated lifting surface, an airflow suction system, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm, and an edge-mounted nozzle bar lowered to sweep debris. I then stated the supported limit of its teaching, that it lifts articles away from a work surface and cleans that surface, so it does not bear on holding a vibrating tool against a covering element already bedded in bonding material.

I made no change to claim 1. Its distinguishing combination stays as drafted: a rigid low-friction perimeter member that deliberately leaves a clearance admitting ambient air, an extraction rate high enough to keep the chamber sub-atmospheric under that continuous ingress, and a wholly rigid transmission path to a bearing face that slides while the differential is maintained. US-11408462-B2 and US-4934475-A both rely on a compliant partition or seal member, US-10001245-B2 surrenders the vacuum coupling to move on an air cushion, DE-202021002652-U1 uses rubber-elastic suction cups, and US-11247858-B2 is lifting and cleaning equipment; none of them holds by a sustained differential across a deliberately leaking rigid perimeter while sliding.
changes: figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md: the grip now rises from the slab's top face, its two lower ends meeting that face; the top-face sentence admits that junction; the handle 44 entry describes the connection as a depiction convention asserting no particular handle form or mounting structure.

figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md: replaced the clause excluding any connection route with one broken line running from inside the housing to chamber 22 indicating the fluid communication schematically, no passage, duct or opening depicted; adjusted the chamber 22 endpoint to stay clear of that line; condensed geometry wording to bring the brief to 2799 characters.
draft/07-drawings.md: the FIG. 2 sentence now lists the fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism and the chamber among the items shown schematically.

figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md: replaced 'one rectangular ring and nothing else' with the perimeter member 24 as one rectangular ring and, within it, the second side 16 as a plain open field, no other body drawn.
draft/08-detailed-description.md: deleted the sentence of meta-commentary following 'The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.'

draft/09-claims.md: claim 10's vibration transmission path is recast from a dangling 'and a vibration transmission path ...' element into the same 'wherein' form used in claim 1, with identical substance.

draft/05-background.md: added a passage citing [REF:US-11247858-B2], the only listed reference previously uncited, describing its suction plate, airflow suction system, lifter actuation system and sweeping nozzle bar, and stating why lifting and cleaning equipment does not bear on holding a vibrating tool against a laid covering element.
data.prior_art_strategy: Claim 1 rests on three features working together, and each carries it clear of a different reference. The perimeter member is rigid, of low-friction material, and deliberately not a seal: a clearance remains along at least part of it through which ambient air enters continuously. US-11408462-B2 forms the peripheral wall of its decompressed space from elastic partitions whose end contacts the wall surface, adding a rigid frame member only to stop the elastic partition being sucked inward, and US-4934475-A uses a seal member that defines its pressure reduction space; both keep compliance in the boundary, which is exactly what the claimed perimeter excludes. DE-202021002652-U1 puts rubber-elastic aprons on suction cups at the ends of vibrated shafts, so the compliance sits directly in the vibration path. Second, the air-extraction mechanism must withdraw air at a rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric while air keeps entering, which is a steady-state leaking condition none of the references describes; each of them instead works toward a closed or sealed space. Third, holding and sliding are simultaneous: the bearing face is slidable while the differential is maintained. US-10001245-B2 is the reference that comes closest to motion under vacuum, and it teaches the opposite trade, switching its pneumatic generator from suction mode to blower mode so the assembly rides an air cushion, that is, giving up the vacuum coupling in order to move. US-4934475-A likewise spends its vibration on reducing the suction-adhering force and driving the body along the wall, rather than delivering vibration into the surface as working output. US-11247858-B2 is peripheral: it is plate handling equipment that lifts sheet material and sweeps debris with nozzles, so the Background states only that supported teaching and why it does not bear on the claimed combination. The specification explains, before it is needed, why the clearance is a design condition rather than a defect and why every compliant member in the load path costs energy that was meant for the covering element, which is the technical problem the combination solves.

content.text:
The single finding is fixed.

**FIG. 1 handle mounting** (`figures/FIG-1-...md:9,11,22`): the brief no longer prescribes a connection topology. The geometry paragraph now says the slab carries "a grip carried above them"; the top-face sentence reads "where the grip does not overlie it"; and the handle 44 entry draws the grip as one closed outline enclosing an open area with "the place at which it meets the machine being shown schematically, no particular handle form, number of connections, attachment location or attachment formation being shown." That mirrors the treatment FIG. 5 already gives the pulling-element attachment, and it removes the self-contradiction in the old sentence, which prescribed a two-ended mounting to the top face while claiming to assert none.

The grip is still carried on the machine, so the sheet does not regress to a detached handle floating over the device, but nothing about how it attaches is now specified. FIG. 1 remains at 2798 characters, under the limit.

No other file needed a change: `draft/07-drawings.md`, `draft/08-detailed-description.md`, `draft/09-claims.md` and `draft/numerals.md` were already neutral as to the handle's form and mounting, and the claims, numeral table, and the other four figure briefs are untouched.

input.summary: Removed the untraced handle mounting topology from the FIG. 1 brief. The grip is still carried on the machine, but its form, number of connections, and attachment location are now shown schematically with nothing specified, matching the treatment FIG. 5 already gives the pulling-element attachment. No change was needed to the claims, description, drawing descriptions, numeral table, or the other four figure briefs.
reasoning: The finding was correct on the substance. The disclosure says only that 'The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface'. It gives no form, no count of connections, and no attachment location, so 'two lower ends meet the top face of the slab' was a connection and a relative position invented to satisfy the previous turn's finding about a floating grip. Number of attachment points and the face they land on are technical substance, not depiction convention, so the schematic label did not cover them.

The old sentence was also self-defeating: it prescribed an exact mounting and then declared that no mounting structure was asserted. A reviewer reading it either follows the prescription, which adds unsupported matter, or follows the disclaimer, which leaves the instruction empty. Replacing both halves with one consistent statement removes that ambiguity.

The repair had to keep the grip attached to the machine in some sense, because the earlier finding that the grip floated free was itself a real defect against the brief's single-silhouette instruction and against claim 8, which recites the handle as a component of the device. The resolution that satisfies both findings is the one FIG. 5 already uses for the pulling element: state that the grip is carried on the machine and that the place where it meets the machine is schematic, with no attachment location or formation shown. Attachment exists; its geometry is unspecified.

Two supporting phrases had to move with it. The geometry paragraph said the grip 'rises from that top face', which is the same untraced topology stated a second time, and the top-face sentence said the face is open 'where the grip does not meet it', which presumes a junction on that face. They now read 'a grip carried above them' and 'where the grip does not overlie it', which describe only what is visible in the view.

Nothing outside this one brief was touched. draft/07-drawings.md calls the handle schematic without describing it, draft/08-detailed-description.md says only that the device may include one or more handles arranged to guide it, claim 8 recites a handle arranged to guide the device, and numerals.md maps 44 to 'handle'. All four were already free of form and mounting detail, so widening or narrowing them to match a drawing would have been the wrong direction of repair. FIG. 1 remains at 2798 characters, inside the 2800 limit.

figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md line 11: 'where the grip does not meet it' becomes 'where the grip does not overlie it'.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn, which touched one figure brief only. Claim 1 continues to rest on three cooperating features. The perimeter member is rigid and of low-friction material and deliberately not a seal, leaving a clearance along at least part of it through which ambient air enters continuously; US-11408462-B2 forms its peripheral wall from elastic partitions and adds a rigid frame only to stop the partition collapsing inward, and US-4934475-A uses a seal member to define its pressure reduction space, so both keep compliance in the boundary the claim requires to be rigid, and DE-202021002652-U1 places rubber-elastic suction cup aprons directly in the vibrated path. The extraction rate must hold the chamber below atmospheric while air keeps entering, a steady leaking condition none of the references describes, each working instead toward a closed space. Holding and sliding are simultaneous, the bearing face being slidable while the differential is maintained; US-10001245-B2 is closest on motion under vacuum and teaches the opposite exchange, switching its pneumatic generator to blower mode and riding an air cushion, so the coupling is surrendered to move, while US-4934475-A spends its vibration on reducing suction-adhering force and driving the body along the wall rather than delivering it into the surface as working output. US-11247858-B2 is peripheral plate handling and cleaning equipment, and the Background states only that supported teaching and why it does not bear on the claimed combination. The handle is a dependent-claim feature and carries no distinguishing weight, which is why holding its geometry unspecified costs the application nothing.

**View:** Plan view looking straight up at the underside of the machine, nothing beneath the machine being drawn. Outline line work only, every outline one thin unbroken line. **Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the perimeter member 24 as one rectangular ring, and within it the second side 16 as a plain open field; no other body is drawn. The ring is the perimeter member 24 seen end on: a closed band with a rectangular opening through it, shown schematically with a rectangular plan outline, this being a depiction convention for this sheet only.

The ring is drawn with two closed thin lines and those two alone, its outer edge and its inner edge, both rectangular. The inner rectangle sits concentrically within the outer one, its four sides parallel to and evenly spaced from the corresponding sides of the outer rectangle, so that the band between them is of the same generous width along all four sides and forms a broad continuous surface running all the way round.

The ring occupies the middle of the drawing area and stands well in from every side of it, with a wide expanse of empty paper separating the outer rectangle from each limit of the drawing area, so that the outer rectangle reads plainly as the edge of the ring. No border, frame or other line follows or approaches the edges of the sheet, and neither rectangle is drawn near them.

Because this view looks straight up at the underside of the machine, the outer edge of the slab above the ring coincides with the outer edge of the ring, that one line serving as the outline of both.

29	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the bearing face 26 bears on the exposed face 38, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn, which touched two figure briefs and one descriptive cross-reference. Claim 1 still rests on three cooperating features. US-11247858-B2 is peripheral plate handling and cleaning equipment, and the Background states only its supported teaching and why it does not bear on the claimed combination. The single finding is fixed.

**FIG. 5 numeral 10 endpoint** (`figures/FIG-5-...md:15`): the target no longer names a right-hand side face, which the stated viewpoint from above and to the front left does not show. It now reads "on the length of it that bounds the slab on the right-hand side", which is a length of the outer silhouette that genuinely exists in that view and still keeps the numeral away from the band and from the flexible pulling element 46 running off to the left.

The only remaining side-face reference is FIG. 1's left-hand side face, which is visible from the same front-left viewpoint and is correct as written. Nothing else changed: FIG. 5's view line, the machine's placement on the right-hand part of the tile, the other label sentences, `draft/07-drawings.md`, `draft/08-detailed-description.md`, `draft/09-claims.md` and `draft/numerals.md` are all untouched. FIG. 5 is 2638 characters and every brief remains under the limit.

input.summary: Corrected the numeral 10 endpoint in the FIG. 5 brief so it targets a length of the outer silhouette that the stated viewpoint actually shows, instead of a right-hand side face that is occluded from above and to the front left. No other file changed.
reasoning: The finding was a real endpoint defect confined to one brief. FIG. 5 fixes its viewpoint as 'from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1', which shows the top, front and left faces of a rectangular slab and occludes the right-hand face. The numeral 10 instruction nevertheless named the right-hand side face, so the target either does not exist in the view or implies a face that should not be drawn. Replacing it with the length of the silhouette that bounds the slab on the right keeps the numeral in the same region of the sheet while naming something the viewpoint genuinely produces.

Keeping the numeral on the right-hand side of the machine matters and is why I did not simply mirror FIG. 1's wording. FIG. 5 places the machine on the right-hand part of the tile so that the flexible pulling element 46 has a clear run to the left, and the numeral 10 endpoint has to stay clear of that element and of the band. A left-hand target would have collided with the pulling element's path.

I did not touch the viewpoint, the machine's placement, or any other label. Mirroring the view to make a right-hand face visible would have been the wrong repair: it would rewrite geometry that is already consistent across FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 in order to rescue one endpoint phrase, and the endpoint phrase is the thing that was wrong.

No invention matter is involved. Which face or edge carries a numeral is a drafting convention; the claims, description, Brief Description of the Drawings and numeral table say nothing about it, so nothing outside the brief needed synchronizing. I confirmed the only other side-face reference is FIG. 1's left-hand side face, which is visible from the same front-left viewpoint and is correct as written.
FIG. 5 is now 2638 characters and all five briefs remain under the 2800 limit, so the change required no compensating trims.

US-11247858-B2 is peripheral plate handling and cleaning equipment, and the Background states only its supported teaching and why it does not bear on the claimed combination.

content.text:
All four flagged sheets have rewritten briefs. The common cause was that the artifacts were forbidden by negative instructions ("no rim, no seam, no stray line, one line and not two"), which the renderer kept violating, so I replaced the prohibitions with positive statements of what each surface contains.

**FIG. 1** (rim on the slab top face, seam and doubled contour on the band, stray lines on the tile): one positive rule now covers all three artifacts. Every surface is empty inside its boundary, each face of the slab, the band front, the housing faces and the open tile being bounded by their own edges alone with no line drawn within any of them, every edge one single line, no line parallel and close to another. The old scattered per-surface prohibitions are gone.

**FIG. 3** (three concentric rectangles instead of two): I deleted the sentence saying the slab's outer edge coincides with the ring's outer edge, "that one line serving as the outline of both." It invited exactly the third rectangle that appeared. The brief now states that the whole sheet carries exactly two closed lines, names each one, and states that the enclosed field, the band, and the paper beyond the outer rectangle are all left open.

**FIG. 4** (extra hatched rectangle beside the column, covering element split by a vertical line, lowest band touching the lower limit): the sheet is now specified as four hatched bodies, with each band one single rectangle running the whole way from the left-hand limit to the right-hand limit, closed above and below by one straight line. The split is blocked by a checkable rule: the column's two side lines are the only vertical lines anywhere on the sheet. The paper on both sides of the column is bare down to the uppermost band, which blocks the extra body. "Stands clear of the lower limit" is replaced by the concrete requirement that open unhatched paper lies beneath the lowest band's lower line.

**FIG. 5** (pulling element drawn as two parallel lines): the element is now described as one curved path in the manner of a slack cord, of even thickness, with the numeral targeting that path. The previous stroke-counting language is removed, per the rule that a cord is described as one path rather than by counting outline strokes. FIG. 5 also gets the same positive surface rule as FIG. 1, since it shows the same machine and was at risk of the same rim and seam artifacts.

Every numeral, definition, endpoint and required relationship is preserved: the sheets still carry 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44; 16, 24; 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42; and 10, 24, 36, 46, and the union across the five sheets is still all 16 numerals. All briefs are within the length limit, the longest being FIG. 4 at 2792. The claims, description, numeral table, Brief Description of the Drawings and the FIG. 2 brief are unchanged.

input.summary: Rewrote the FIG. 1, FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 briefs to specify the geometry positively instead of by prohibition, which is the class of instruction the renderer was violating. Removed the FIG. 3 sentence that invited a third rectangle, blocked the FIG. 4 split bands and extra body with a rule about the only vertical lines on the sheet, and described the FIG. 5 pulling element as one curved path rather than by counting strokes. No claim, description sentence, numeral definition or Brief Description entry changed.
reasoning: All four failures were rendered-pixel defects, so the repair belonged in the briefs, not in the invention. What the four had in common is that the violated requirement was stated as a prohibition: no rim or paired contour, no seam line, no stray line, no third rectangle, one line and not two. An image model reproduces the nouns it is given, so naming rims, seams and second lines is close to asking for them. I rewrote each failing constraint as a statement of what the sheet does contain, which is checkable in the same way but does not name the artifact.

FIG. 1 had three separate complaints, all of them lines drawn inside a surface that should be blank. One rule now covers them: every surface is empty inside its boundary, each face of the slab, the band front, the housing faces and the open tile bounded by their own edges alone, every edge one single line, and no line parallel and close to another. That last clause is what a doubled rim contour is, described without naming a rim.

The FIG. 3 third rectangle had an identifiable cause in the brief. A sentence said the slab's outer edge coincides with the ring's outer edge, one line serving as the outline of both, which tells a renderer there are two coincident outlines and invites it to draw them a few pixels apart. Nothing depends on that sentence, so I deleted it and replaced the counting language with an explicit inventory: exactly two closed lines, each named, with the enclosed field, the band and the surrounding paper all left open.

FIG. 4 failed three ways that share one fix. Specifying each band as one single rectangle running the whole way from the left-hand limit to the right-hand limit, closed above and below by one straight line, prevents the covering element being split, and stating that the column's two side lines are the only vertical lines on the sheet makes the split and the extra hatched body beside the column both violations of one short checkable rule. I also replaced 'the lowest band stands clear of the lower limit', which the renderer ignored, with the concrete positive form: open unhatched paper lies beneath the lowest band's lower line.

For FIG. 5 the drawing rules themselves say a cord is described as one curved path and never by counting outline strokes or by a white interior. The old brief did exactly what is forbidden, saying one line and not two with no interior between lines, and got two parallel lines back. It is now one curved path in the manner of a slack cord, of even thickness, and the numeral targets that path. I gave FIG. 5 the same positive surface rule as FIG. 1 because it shows the same machine and was carrying the same rim and seam prohibitions that failed on FIG. 1.

I kept every numeral, definition, endpoint and relationship intact and took the length back out of wording that carried no relationship, so all five briefs stay within the limit. Nothing in draft/ moved: which lines a renderer draws inside a face has no bearing on the claims, the description, the numeral table or the Brief Description of the Drawings, and changing any of them to accommodate the pixels would have been the wrong direction of repair.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn, which touched four figure briefs only. Claim 1 continues to rest on three cooperating features. A rigid low-friction perimeter member that is deliberately not a seal leaves a clearance along at least part of it through which ambient air enters continuously, separating it from US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is formed by elastic partitions with a rigid frame added only to stop the partition collapsing inward, from US-4934475-A, which uses a seal member to define its pressure reduction space, and from DE-202021002652-U1, which places rubber-elastic suction cup aprons directly in the vibrated path. The extraction rate must hold the chamber below atmospheric while air keeps entering, a steady leaking condition none of the references describes, each working toward a closed space instead. Holding and sliding are simultaneous, the bearing face being slidable while the differential is maintained, where US-10001245-B2 teaches the opposite exchange by switching its pneumatic generator to blower mode and riding an air cushion, surrendering the vacuum coupling in order to move, and US-4934475-A spends its vibration on reducing suction-adhering force and driving the body along the wall rather than delivering it into the surface as working output. US-11247858-B2 is peripheral plate handling and cleaning equipment, and the Background states only its supported teaching and why it does not bear on the claimed combination. FIG. 4 remains the sheet that shows the clearance admitting ambient air beneath a bearing face that elsewhere along the loop bears rigidly on the covering element, which is why its geometry had to be made renderable rather than relaxed.
